answer_text:
## AltaVista: The Rise and Fall of a Search Pioneer

**AltaVista** was one of the most important and influential search engines in the history of the internet. Here's the full story:

---

### 🚀 Origins (1995)
AltaVista was created by researchers at Digital Equipment Corporation (DEC) who were trying to showcase the company's hardware and make it easier to find files on the company's public network. Launched in December 1995, it was the first "full text"/boolean searchable index of the World Wide Web.

At launch, AltaVista had two innovations that put it ahead of other search engines: it used a fast, multi-threaded web crawler called Scooter that could cover many more web pages than were believed to exist at the time, and it had an efficient backend database, TurboVista, running on advanced hardware.

---

### 📈 Peak Popularity
Web traffic increased steadily from 300,000 hits on the first day to more than 80 million hits per day by 1997, making it one of the most popular websites at the time.

As late as 2000, it was still more popular than Google, holding 17.7% of the search market compared to Google's 7%. In 1997, it also launched Babel Fish, a web-based machine translation application that translated text or webpages — an early forerunner of Google Translate.

---

### 📉 The Decline
In 1998, Digital was sold to Compaq, and in 1999, Compaq redesigned AltaVista as a Web portal. Under CEO Rod Schrock, it abandoned its streamlined search page and transformed itself into a web portal, diluting its core search function with features like shopping and email.

This backfired drastically. By focusing on becoming a full-fledged web portal, AltaVista diluted its core strength: search.

By the early 2000s, AltaVista was spiraling. The dot-com bubble burst, its IPO was canceled, and its user base shrank.

---

### 🔄 A Series of Acquisitions
In June 1999, Compaq sold 83% of AltaVista to CMGI for $2.1 billion in stock and $220 million in cash. In February 2003, Overture Services acquired AltaVista for $140 million. In July 2003, Yahoo acquired Overture for $1.63 billion.

From that point on, AltaVista became a zombie brand — a shell that used Yahoo!'s search technology but maintained its old look. No innovation, no updates, no real purpose.

---

### 💀 The End (2013)
The official closure happened quietly on July 8, 2013. No farewell. No headlines. Just a redirect to Yahoo.com.

---

### 🏆 Legacy
AltaVista failed because of its alternating ownership, a failed shift towards becoming a portal, and because its core search business was eventually overtaken by Google. Despite its fall, AltaVista is credited with implementing the first CAPTCHA to prevent fraudulent account registrations and internet bots from automatically adding pages to its web index. It remains a landmark in internet history — the search engine that helped define what online search could be, before Google made it ubiquitous.
